steps.explanationAfterStep: A Diels–Alder reaction with a C=O as the dienophile: two new σ bonds (C–C and C–O) and one new π bond, in one step. The two oxygens make Danishefsky's diene so nucleophilic that even an unactivated aldehyde reacts; the lanthanide Lewis acid binds the carbonyl oxygen and makes it more electrophilic. Regiochemistry follows the largest orbital coefficients: the CH₂ end of the diene to the carbonyl carbon. (With strong Lewis acids such as BF₃ or ZnCl₂ the same product can form stepwise, by a Mukaiyama aldol and then ring closure.)
The methoxy group of the cyclic acetal is protonated, turning it into a good leaving group (methanol).

Methanol leaves, pushed out through the ring C=C by the silyloxy oxygen. The cation is shared over both oxygens: the ring oxygen can push to the same carbon, so drawing it from there gives a resonance form of the same cation. Eliminating methanol makes the C=C conjugated with what will be the ketone.

Trifluoroacetate takes the silyl group, leaving the neutral enone (a vinylogous ester: the ring oxygen donates into the C=O). Overall the diene has delivered a ketone and the aldehyde carbon is now a ring CH next to oxygen: the product is 2-phenyl-2,3-dihydro-4H-pyran-4-one.

title: Hetero-Diels–Alder reaction of Danishefsky's diene
subtitle: A C=O is the dienophile; acid then reveals a dihydropyranone
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 34
Fleming, Pericyclic Reactions, 2nd edition (Oxford Chemistry Primers, Oxford University Press)
Bednarski and Danishefsky, J. Am. Chem. Soc., 1983, 105, 3716

adduct.caption: the cycloadduct: a 2-phenyl-3,6-dihydro-2H-pyran with a silyl enol ether and a methoxy acetal

cation.caption: the conjugated oxocarbenium ion (shared over both oxygens) + methanol + trifluoroacetate
hintTiers: Silicon is the Lewis acidic atom of the cation's silyloxy group, and oxygen binds silicon strongly. Which species can take the silyl group?
The trifluoroacetate oxygen bonds to silicon, and the Si–O bond to the ring oxygen breaks, leaving C=O. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: from a lone pair of the negative trifluoroacetate oxygen to a new bond to silicon. Arrow 2: from the bond between silicon and the positive oxygen to a lone pair on that oxygen.
cation.learnerPrompt: Trifluoroacetate removes the silyl group. Draw the step that gives the neutral ketone.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Adding to the C=O⁺ carbon is possible but reversible and goes nowhere. The silyl group is what has to come off: trifluoroacetate bonds to silicon.
A methyl group on silicon is not an electrophile. Trifluoroacetate bonds to silicon itself, which can take a fifth ligand on the way.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: trifluoroacetate bonds to silicon. Silicon now has five bonds, so in the same step the Si–O bond to the ring breaks. One more arrow.

reactants.caption: Danishefsky's diene (trans-1-methoxy-3-trimethylsilyloxybuta-1,3-diene) + benzaldehyde
hintTiers: This diene carries two electron-donating oxygens, so it is very nucleophilic; the C=O is the electron-poor partner. Which end of the diene is most nucleophilic, and which atom of the C=O is the electrophile?

The CH₂ end of the diene bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and the carbonyl oxygen bonds to the other end of the diene, the carbon carrying the methoxy group. Three arrows round the ring, as in any Diels–Alder.

Arrow 1: from the CH₂=C π bond to a new bond between the CH₂ and the carbonyl carbon. Arrow 2: from the other diene π bond to the bond between the two middle carbons of the diene. Arrow 3: from the C=O π bond to a new bond between the carbonyl oxygen and the methoxy-bearing carbon.
reactants.learnerPrompt: The C=O of benzaldehyde acts as the dienophile. Draw the cycloaddition that makes a six-membered ring containing oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That puts the carbonyl oxygen on the CH₂ end of the diene. The CH₂ end is the nucleophilic one (both oxygens push electrons to it), so it bonds to the electrophilic carbonyl carbon; the oxygen ends up on the methoxy-bearing carbon.
The silyloxy oxygen pushes electrons into the diene, but it does not bond to anything in this step. The new bonds form at the two ends of the diene.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the nucleophilic end of the diene bonds to the carbonyl carbon. In the same concerted step the π bonds move round and the carbonyl oxygen bonds to the far end of the diene. Two more arrows.

protonated.caption: the methoxy group protonated + trifluoroacetate
hintTiers: A cation forms as methanol leaves. Which oxygen lone pair can reach the carbon that loses methanol, directly or through the ring C=C?

The silyl enol ether pushes through the ring: the silyloxy oxygen's lone pair makes C=O⁺, the ring C=C moves along, and methanol leaves with its pair. Three arrows. (Pushing with the ring oxygen gives another resonance form of the same cation, and also counts.)

Arrow 1: from a lone pair of the silyloxy oxygen to its bond with the ring carbon (a new π bond). Arrow 2: from the ring C=C π bond to the bond between the next two carbons, ending at the carbon that carries the methoxy group. Arrow 3: from the bond between that carbon and the protonated methoxy oxygen to a lone pair on that oxygen.
protonated.learnerPrompt: Methanol leaves. Which lone pair pushes it out?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking the methyl–oxygen bond would make a methyl cation, which never happens here. The ring carbon–oxygen bond breaks, because the ring cation is stabilised by both oxygens.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: methanol leaves. Do not leave a bare cation on its own: in the same step a lone pair pushes it out, either from the ring oxygen or, through the C=C, from the silyloxy oxygen.

adduct-and-acid.caption: the cycloadduct + trifluoroacetic acid
hintTiers: The ring carbon next to the ring oxygen also carries a methoxy group: it is an acetal carbon. What does an acetal need to lose one of its OR groups?
Protonate the methoxy oxygen, so that methanol can later leave. Two arrows: a proton transfer.
Arrow 1: from a lone pair of the methoxy oxygen to a new bond to the acidic H of trifluoroacetic acid. Arrow 2: from the O–H bond of the acid to a lone pair on its oxygen.
adduct-and-acid.learnerPrompt: Trifluoroacetic acid unmasks the ketone. First, which oxygen does the acid protonate?

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Protonating the ring oxygen would open the ring, which is not what happens. Protonate the methoxy oxygen: methanol is the group that leaves.
Protonating the silyl enol ether at carbon is how a simple silyl enol ether is hydrolysed, but here the acetal goes first: protonate the methoxy oxygen so that methanol can leave.

mechanismSummary: Danishefsky's diene (trans-1-methoxy-3-trimethylsilyloxybuta-1,3-diene) is electron-rich enough to react with the C=O of an ordinary aldehyde in a hetero-Diels–Alder reaction, here with a mild lanthanide Lewis acid, Eu(fod)₃. The CH₂ end of the diene bonds to the carbonyl carbon and the carbonyl oxygen to the methoxy-bearing end. Acid then does three things in a row: protonates the methoxy group, loses methanol to a cation stabilised by both oxygens, and removes the silyl group. The result is a 2,3-dihydro-4H-pyran-4-one, a ring found in many natural products; with a chiral catalyst the new stereocentre can be set in one enantiomer. With strong Lewis acids the cycloaddition can be stepwise (Mukaiyama aldol, then cyclisation); the product is the same. The Lewis acid catalyst is not drawn. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the drawings carry no wedges.
